title: Giving the Agent a Body and a Browser
description: Eight tools that decide where an agent runs and what it is allowed to touch, from desktop agents and sandboxes to typed browser control.
content:
# Giving the Agent a Body and a Browser

A model with no tools is a very fast writer of prose. Everything interesting happens once it can click, run, render or order something — and that is also where every risk lives.

The eight tools here are not competing. They each draw the boundary in a different place: some give the agent a whole computer, some give it one carefully indexed page, and one gives it a PCB quote.

## A computer, not a chat box

[[link:/tools/2213|Wavefunction]] is a macOS coding agent built on the opposite instinct to every other agent app. Where competitors add tabs, sidebars, editor panels and a terminal, this one keeps a project sidebar and a conversation. The agent splits work across subagents in their own worktrees so you can send the next task while the last runs, and when it needs a desktop it uses its own inside a local Docker container rather than yours. Free and MIT licensed, with local models, your own keys or a ChatGPT sign-in.

[[link:/tools/2245|PhreshOS]] goes further and asks what an operating system looks like when its users are programs. It is an open-source, self-hosted system for apps built with web technologies: the System runs on your machine, gives each Program a place to run, one sign-in, storage, inter-Program communication and per-Program permissions. Everything on the Desktop — the file manager, Settings, the wallpaper — is itself a Program built on the System. It is explicitly experimental, and worth reading for the architecture alone.

## Containment

[[link:/tools/2231|Drop Sandbox]] is the answer to the specific fear of running an agent with permissions skipped. It is a rootless Linux sandbox built on your existing distribution rather than containers, so every program you already installed is available inside, but each environment has its own home directory while the real one stays hidden. A hallucinated rm -rf does not reach your files, a prompt injection aimed at ~/.ssh finds nothing, and localhost services are refused. TOML config decides what gets exposed, and gVisor is available as an extra layer.

## The browser, indexed

[[link:/tools/2242|Jev Browser]] is the most interesting design in this group. Instead of screenshots, a skill lists every control the page offers; Jev picks one operation and target from that table and states its confidence. The answer is validated as a key into the table, so anything outside it throws before anything runs. Jev never writes text — you supply the strings and it picks which goes where — and a secret only goes into password fields. The whole thing is MIT licensed, stateless, and costs a few thousand input tokens per step.

[[link:/tools/2226|fastbrowse]] builds on the same idea for production work. It returns cited answers or schema-validated data, with the quoted page text the answer came from. Credentials are passed by name and resolved only on the allowed origin, so a password never enters a prompt, and actions classified as irreversible pause for approval unless the caller authorised them. Its published demo run logs 19 steps, 41 seconds and five cents of model cost, unrounded.

## Rendering and ordering

[[link:/tools/2214|Recto]] gives a coding agent a visual canvas. It detects the agents installed on your machine, runs their CLIs inside its own window, and lets you select an element and move it yourself or reprompt — for UI, SVG, motion and 3D. It is free and native on Windows, Mac and Linux.

[[link:/tools/2246|Blender Copilot]] applies the same logic inside Blender: a chat panel whose agent loop runs in Blender's own Python process, executing the model's bpy against your live scene, with the whole turn wrapped in one Ctrl+Z. No bridge, no sidecar, no stale copy of the scene. It is at four stars, so treat it as a shape worth watching.

[[link:/tools/2241|ProvenMetal MCP]] is the most concrete endpoint here. Connect an assistant and it quotes and orders assembled PCBs: JLCPCB rates plus assembly, parts, shipping and import charges, with what each option adds or saves shown before you pay. No account needed to start, and an order can be repriced with changes in one step.

## What the boundary decides

Two of these tools give the agent a general computer and accept the consequences. Two constrain it to a validated list of controls. Two give it a rendering surface. One gives it a manufacturing order.

The pattern worth noting is that the interesting design work has moved from the model to the interface. [[link:/tools/2242|Jev Browser]] is not better because of a better model; it is better because the page was reduced to a table the model cannot escape. [[link:/tools/2231|Drop Sandbox]] is not safer because of a smarter filter; it is safer because the filesystem was never mounted.

If you are building with agents this quarter, the question to answer first is not which model. It is what the agent is allowed to touch, and whether you can prove afterwards that it stayed inside that line.
tldr: An agent is only as useful as the surface it can reach. Wavefunction, Recto, Jev Browser, fastbrowse, Drop Sandbox, Blender Copilot, PhreshOS and ProvenMetal MCP each answer a different version of that question.
